questions.q: What does header=True do when reading a CSV in PySpark?
options: Treats the file's first row as real column names instead of naming columns _c0, _c1, etc.
Deletes the first row of the file entirely
Forces every column to be read as a string
Has no effect unless inferSchema is also set
questions.explain: Without it, Spark auto-names columns _c0, _c1, _c2, and treats the header row as data.

questions.q: What does inferSchema=True actually cost, under the hood?
options: Spark reads the file a second time: once to guess column types, once to actually load the data
Nothing — it's free and instant regardless of file size
It only works on files smaller than 1MB
It converts the file to JSON first
questions.explain: This is a real, measurable cost, which is why production pipelines often pass an explicit schema instead.

questions.q: If you skip inferSchema entirely, how does every column come back?
options: As a string, regardless of what the actual data looks like
As whatever type Spark guesses is most likely
The read fails with an error
As integers only
questions.explain: Without inferSchema, Spark makes no attempt to detect numeric or date types — everything defaults to string.

questions.q: Why doesn't spark.read.csv() alone actually load any data yet?
options: Because of lazy evaluation — read.csv() builds a plan, and only an action like .show() or .count() actually triggers the read
Because CSV files require a separate unlock command first
Because Spark always waits exactly 5 seconds before reading
It does load all the data immediately, with no exceptions
questions.explain: This connects straight back to Lesson 34's lazy evaluation: transformations build a plan, actions execute it.

questions.q: Why do production pipelines often pass an explicit schema instead of using inferSchema=True?
options: To avoid the cost of a full extra read pass over a large file just to guess types
Because inferSchema is deprecated and no longer works
Because explicit schemas are required by law for financial data
There's no real reason — it's purely a stylistic choice
questions.explain: On large files, the double-read cost of inferSchema adds up — Lesson 43 covers writing an explicit schema directly.
